data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's diagnostic criterion—divergence between panel and expert on items requiring an expert-unique, outcome-determinative cue—cannot distinguish a genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance within a single evaluation, because the diagnostic is symmetric with respect to the competing explanation it is meant to separate. If the panel outperforms the expert on expert-unique items, that could mean the checklist genuinely captured the expert's cue-set; but it could equally mean the checklist's mechanical compliance with a surface correlate happens to beat the expert's noisy intuition on those very items. Conversely, if the expert outperforms the panel, that could mean the checklist omitted a genuine cue, or that the expert's intuition is merely tracking a different heuristic that happens to be correlated. The target never identifies what within the single evaluation would break this symmetry: it asserts that the divergence 'reveals whether the checklist has merely tracked the easy cases or genuinely captured the expert's cue-set,' but the divergence pattern alone does not adjudicate between these mechanisms unless one has independent ground truth about which cues are genuinely outcome-determinative versus merely correlated—an external standard the target never requires.
